topics.name: Gettysburg Address
topics.kicker: Lincoln’s 1863 cemetery speech · Begins “Four score and seven years ago”
topics.briefing: On November 19, 1863, Abraham Lincoln stood near a Pennsylvania battlefield where thousands of soldiers had died that July and spoke for only about two minutes. The main speaker, Edward Everett, had just talked for two hours, yet it is Lincoln’s fewer than 300 words, from “Four score and seven years ago” to “government of the people, by the people, for the people,” that students still memorize.
topics.answerHtml: Gettysburg Address (accept descriptions like Lincoln’s speech at Gettysburg; prompt on Gettysburg)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The day after this speech, the main orator at the same ceremony wrote to its author that he wished he had come as close to “the central idea of the occasion” in two hours as this speech had in two minutes. That orator was Edward Everett.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this short 1863 speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: Five handwritten copies of this speech survive, each named for the person who received it, including John Nicolay, John Hay, and George Bancroft. The only copy its author signed, the Bliss copy, is displayed in the Lincoln Bedroom of the White House.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this speech that ends by hoping that “government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.”

tossups.p: Garry Wills won a Pulitzer Prize for a book about this speech subtitled _The Words That Remade America_. This speech had fewer than 300 words and took only about two minutes to deliver.
tossups.r: Its speaker hoped for “a new birth of freedom.” For 10 points, name this speech that Abraham Lincoln gave at a soldiers’ cemetery in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: A local lawyer named David Wills invited this speech’s author to make “a few appropriate remarks,” and the speaker spent the night before in Wills’s house on the town square. In this speech, he honored men who gave “the last full measure of devotion.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this speech that Abraham Lincoln delivered at a Pennsylvania cemetery in November 1863.

tossups.p: This speech never mentions slavery, the Confederacy, or even the town where it was given. Its speaker said that he and his listeners “can not consecrate” or “hallow” the ground, because the brave men “living and dead” who struggled there had already done so.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: Near the start of his “I Have a Dream” speech, Martin Luther King Jr. echoed this earlier speech with the words “Five score years ago.” The full text of this speech is carved inside the Lincoln Memorial, where King spoke, along with its author’s Second Inaugural Address.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this speech in which Abraham Lincoln called for “a new birth of freedom” in 1863.

tossups.p: Soon after giving this speech, its author came down with varioloid [“VAIR-ee-uh-loyd”], a mild form of smallpox. In the speech, he predicted that “the world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this speech that Abraham Lincoln gave at the dedication of a national cemetery in 1863.

tossups.p: This speech says that it is “for us the living” to be dedicated to “the unfinished work” that those who fought there had “thus far so nobly advanced.” It describes a “great civil war” testing whether a nation “so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this short speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: Its speaker described the fallen soldiers as “those who here gave their lives that that nation might live,” and he urged the living to “take increased devotion” from these “honored dead.” This speech followed a two-hour oration by Edward Everett.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this speech that Abraham Lincoln delivered to dedicate a soldiers’ cemetery in November 1863.

tossups.p: Its speaker said it was “altogether fitting and proper” to set aside part of a battlefield as “a final resting place” for those who died there. Its first sentence describes a new nation “conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this short speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: The opening words of this speech count back eighty-seven years, to 1776, dating the nation’s birth to the Declaration of Independence rather than to the Constitution. Its author had ridden a train from Washington the day before he delivered it.
tossups.r: Edward Everett spoke for two hours before it. For 10 points, name this speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: Its speaker called on his audience to take up “the great task remaining before us” and to “highly resolve that these dead shall not have died in vain.” He wanted the nation to have “a new birth of freedom.”
tossups.r: He spoke on a field where armies had fought for three days that July. For 10 points, name this November 1863 speech by Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: A former Secretary of State and president of Harvard gave the main oration at the ceremony where this speech was delivered. The next day, this speech’s author wrote to him that “you could not have been excused to make a short address, nor I a long one.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this two-minute speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

tossups.p: This speech’s author told his audience, “We are met on a great battle-field of that war,” and said that brave men had consecrated the ground “far above our poor power to add or detract.” His formal invitation to speak had arrived less than three weeks earlier.
tossups.r: It was given on November 19, 1863. For 10 points, name this speech that Abraham Lincoln gave to dedicate a cemetery in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: In a 2014 documentary by Ken Burns, students at a small school in Vermont work for weeks to memorize and recite this speech. Generations of American schoolchildren have also learned its call for “a new birth of freedom.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this speech by Abraham Lincoln that begins “Four score and seven years ago.”

trap.title: Speech, not battle
trap.body: Gettysburg was both a three-day battle (July 1–3, 1863) and the place where Abraham Lincoln gave this speech that November. Battle tossups often end by mentioning the speech, and speech tossups mention the battle, so it is easy to answer the wrong one. Saying just “Gettysburg” on a speech question earns only a prompt, and “Battle of Gettysburg” is wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this speech” or “this address” wants the Gettysburg Address, while “this battle” wants the Battle of Gettysburg. Quotes like “Four score” or “a new birth of freedom” mean this speech; Lincoln’s Second Inaugural (“with malice toward none”) and his “House Divided” speech are different answers.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gettysburg Address (accept descriptions like Lincoln’s speech at Gettysburg; prompt on Gettysburg)

topics.name: Grover Cleveland
topics.kicker: 22nd and 24th U.S. President · First to serve two non-consecutive terms
topics.briefing: Grover Cleveland is counted twice in the list of presidents: he was the 22nd president, lost the 1888 election, and then won again to become the 24th, the first president to serve two non-consecutive terms. A stubborn New York Democrat who vetoed hundreds of bills, he married 21-year-old Frances Folsom in the White House and once had secret surgery on a yacht so the country would not panic.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This president vetoed a bill to spend ten thousand dollars on seed for drought-stricken farmers in Texas, writing that “though the people support the Government, the Government should not support the people.” He also vetoed hundreds of private pension bills for Civil War veterans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat from New York who served as both the 22nd and 24th president.

tossups.p: In 1893, this president secretly had a tumor removed from the roof of his mouth during an operation aboard the yacht _Oneida_, and the operation was not publicly confirmed until 1917. He kept it quiet because the country was already in a financial panic.
tossups.r: That Panic of 1893 hurt his second term, which began four years after his first ended. For 10 points, name this president who served two non-consecutive terms.

tossups.p: A California Republican pretending to be a British-born voter named Charles Murchison tricked the British minister, Lionel Sackville-West, into writing a letter that favored this man in the 1888 election. Newspapers printed the letter, which hurt this man with Irish American voters.
tossups.r: He lost that election to Benjamin Harrison but beat Harrison four years later. For 10 points, name this 22nd and 24th president.

tossups.p: Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld protested when this president sent federal troops into Chicago in 1894, saying they were needed to keep the U.S. mail moving. That action helped break a nationwide railroad boycott led by Eugene Debs’s American Railway Union.
tossups.r: That conflict was the Pullman Strike. For 10 points, name this president, the first to serve two non-consecutive terms.

tossups.p: After a group led by American businessmen and planters overthrew Queen Liliuokalani [“lih-lee-oo-oh-kuh-LAH-nee”], this president sent James Blount to investigate, withdrew a treaty to annex Hawaii, and called for the queen to be restored. Hawaii was not annexed until William McKinley’s presidency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who was president from 1885 to 1889 and again from 1893 to 1897.

tossups.p: During a boundary dispute between Venezuela and British Guiana, this president’s Secretary of State, Richard Olney, claimed that under the Monroe Doctrine the United States was “practically sovereign” on its continent. Britain finally agreed to settle the dispute through arbitration.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who served two non-consecutive terms, from 1885 to 1889 and from 1893 to 1897.

tossups.p: In 1887, this president signed the Interstate Commerce Act, which set up the first federal agency to regulate railroads, and the Dawes Act, which divided reservation land into plots for individual Native American families. That same year, he vetoed the Dependent Pension Bill.
tossups.r: He later became the first president to serve two non-consecutive terms. For 10 points, name this Democrat from New York.

tossups.p: At a meeting of ministers supporting this man’s opponent, Samuel Burchard called the Democrats the party of “Rum, Romanism, and Rebellion,” angering Irish Catholic voters in New York. Reform-minded Republicans nicknamed Mugwumps also crossed party lines to back this man.
tossups.r: He narrowly beat James G. Blaine in the election of 1884. For 10 points, name this Democrat who later lost to Benjamin Harrison and then beat him.

tossups.p: To stop gold from draining out of the Treasury, this president called Congress into a special session that repealed the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, and he later made a deal in which J. P. Morgan’s bankers supplied the government with gold. Those moves angered silver supporters in his own party.
tossups.r: In 1896, that party turned to William Jennings Bryan and “free silver.” For 10 points, name this president during the Panic of 1893.

tossups.p: At a ceremony in New York Harbor in October 1886, this president accepted a gift from France, promising that “we will not forget that Liberty has here made her home.” Earlier that year, he had married Frances Folsom in the Blue Room of the White House.
tossups.r: He served as the 22nd president and, after a four-year break, as the 24th. For 10 points, name this Democrat.

tossups.p: This president devoted his entire 1887 annual message to Congress to one issue, calling for lower tariffs, which made tariffs the main issue of the next election. In that election, he won more popular votes than his opponent but lost in the Electoral College.
tossups.r: Four years later, he beat that opponent, Benjamin Harrison. For 10 points, name this 22nd and 24th president.

tossups.p: This man’s motto was “A public office is a public trust,” and he earned the nickname “the veto mayor” for blocking wasteful spending in Buffalo. As governor of New York, he angered the Tammany Hall political machine. His first vice president, Thomas Hendricks, died after less than a year in office.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York Democrat who was elected president in 1884 and again in 1892.

tossups.p: During this president’s second term, Jacob Coxey led an “army” of unemployed workers on a march to Washington, D.C., and a tariff law that included an income tax became law without his signature. The Supreme Court struck down that income tax in 1895.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president during the Panic of 1893, who had first held the office from 1885 to 1889.

tossups.p: The company that made the Baby Ruth candy bar claimed it was named for this president’s daughter Ruth, who was born in 1891. His wife, Frances Folsom, was just 21 when they married, making her the youngest First Lady.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who married in the White House and served as the 22nd and 24th president.

tossups.p: Born in Caldwell, New Jersey, this man spent his last years in Princeton, where he served as a trustee of the university, and his last words were reportedly “I have tried so hard to do right.” His portrait appeared on the $1,000 bill.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who lost the 1888 election to Benjamin Harrison but returned to the White House four years later.

clues.t: Both the 22nd and the 24th President of the United States, a Democrat
First president to serve two non-consecutive terms (1885–1889 and 1893–1897)
Lost the 1888 election to Benjamin Harrison, then beat him in 1892
Married Frances Folsom in the White House’s Blue Room (1886); at 21, she was the youngest First Lady
A Democrat who was mayor of Buffalo and then governor of New York before becoming president
Beat James G. Blaine in 1884, becoming the first Democrat elected president after the Civil War
Vetoed hundreds of bills, including many private pension bills for Civil War veterans and the Dependent Pension Bill (1887)
Sent federal troops to break the Pullman Strike (1894), over the protests of Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld
His second term began with the Panic of 1893, a severe economic depression
Defended the gold standard and got the Sherman Silver Purchase Act repealed; in 1896 his party turned to William Jennings Bryan
Withdrew a treaty to annex Hawaii and called for Queen Liliuokalani to be restored to her throne
Accepted the Statue of Liberty at its dedication in October 1886
Devoted his whole 1887 annual message to Congress to lowering the tariff, the main issue of the 1888 election
Vetoed the Texas Seed Bill (1887): “though the people support the Government, the Government should not support the people”
Had a tumor secretly removed from his mouth aboard the yacht _Oneida_ (1893); the operation was not publicly confirmed until 1917
Signed the Interstate Commerce Act, which regulated railroads, and the Dawes Act, which split up reservation land (both 1887)
Reform Republicans called Mugwumps backed him in 1884; Samuel Burchard’s “Rum, Romanism, and Rebellion” remark hurt Blaine
Murchison letter (1888): a trick got British minister Lionel Sackville-West to favor him in writing, costing him Irish American votes
Venezuela boundary crisis (1895): Secretary of State Richard Olney said the U.S. was “practically sovereign” on its continent
J. P. Morgan’s bankers helped refill the Treasury’s gold reserve (1895)
Coxey’s Army of unemployed workers marched on Washington, D.C., in 1894
The Wilson–Gorman Tariff (1894), which included an income tax, became law without his signature
Motto: “A public office is a public trust”; known as “the veto mayor” of Buffalo; clashed with Tammany Hall
First vice president, Thomas Hendricks, died in 1885; Adlai Stevenson was his vice president in the second term
The maker of the Baby Ruth candy bar claimed it was named for his daughter Ruth, born in 1891
Born in Caldwell, New Jersey; retired to Princeton; last words reportedly “I have tried so hard to do right”
His portrait appeared on the $1,000 bill

trap.title: Two terms, two numbers
trap.body: Grover Cleveland was both the 22nd and the 24th president, so a question can call him either number. Benjamin Harrison, the 23rd president, served between Cleveland’s two terms, beating him in 1888 and losing to him in 1892, so their clues get tangled. In January 2025, Donald Trump, the 45th president, began a second, non-consecutive term as the 47th president, so that fact alone no longer points to just one man.
trap.fix: Cleveland clues: Buffalo, the Texas Seed Bill veto, the White House wedding, the Pullman Strike, the Panic of 1893, and Queen Liliuokalani. Harrison clues: the McKinley Tariff, the Sherman Antitrust Act, and the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, which Cleveland got repealed. Don’t confuse Benjamin Harrison with his grandfather, William Henry Harrison.
trap.line: Real answer line: Grover Cleveland (or Stephen Grover Cleveland)

topics.name: James Madison
topics.kicker: 4th U.S. President · Father of the Constitution and the Bill of Rights
topics.briefing: James Madison was the shortest president, about 5 feet 4 inches tall, but few Americans did more to shape the country. Called the “Father of the Constitution,” he drew up the Virginia Plan, wrote 29 of _The Federalist Papers_ to defend the new Constitution, and wrote the amendments that became the Bill of Rights. As the 4th president, he led the nation through the War of 1812, when the British burned Washington, D.C.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: An amendment this man proposed in 1789, saying that a law changing Congress’s pay cannot take effect until after the next election, was finally ratified in 1992 as the 27th Amendment. It was one of twelve amendments that Congress sent to the states in 1789.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this “Father of the Constitution” who later served as the fourth president of the United States.

tossups.p: In 1789, this man beat future president James Monroe in a race for a seat in the first House of Representatives after he promised voters he would support amendments to the new Constitution. Earlier, he had doubted such amendments would help, calling lists of rights “parchment barriers.”
tossups.r: He then drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights. For 10 points, name this Virginian who became the fourth president.

tossups.p: In one essay, this author argued that a large republic is the best cure for “the mischiefs of faction.” In another, he wrote that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary” and that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition.”
tossups.r: Those essays were _Federalist_ No. 10 and No. 51. For 10 points, name this co-author of _The Federalist Papers_ who became the fourth president.

tossups.p: This delegate’s careful notes are the most complete record of the debates at the Constitutional Convention, but they were not published until 1840, after his death. At that convention, Edmund Randolph presented a plan this man had largely drafted, which based representation in Congress on population.
tossups.r: That plan was the Virginia Plan. For 10 points, name this Virginian known as the “Father of the Constitution.”

tossups.p: Both of this president’s vice presidents died in office: George Clinton in 1812, and Elbridge Gerry, whose name lives on in the word “gerrymander,” in 1814. This president lived and is buried at Montpelier, his family’s plantation in Virginia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fourth president, who led the country during the War of 1812.

tossups.p: Just before leaving office in 1817, this president vetoed John C. Calhoun’s Bonus Bill, which would have paid for roads and canals, because he believed the Constitution did not allow it. A year earlier, he had signed a charter for the Second Bank of the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who had earlier drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights.

tossups.p: In February 1815, this president signed a peace treaty into effect at the Octagon House, a Washington mansion where he and his wife lived after the British burned the White House. That treaty had been signed on Christmas Eve, 1814, by negotiators including Henry Clay and John Quincy Adams.
tossups.r: Federalists had nicknamed the war that treaty ended after this president. For 10 points, name this president during the War of 1812.

tossups.p: Paul Jennings, a man this president enslaved who served him in the White House, later wrote a short book about him that is often called the first White House memoir. Jennings later gained his freedom with help from Senator Daniel Webster.
tossups.r: This president’s wife, Dolley, had a portrait of George Washington rescued when the British burned the White House. For 10 points, name this fourth president.

tossups.p: In 1785, this man’s “Memorial and Remonstrance” argued against a Virginia tax to support teachers of the Christian religion. He then got the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom passed in 1786 while its author, Thomas Jefferson, was in France.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who later wrote the Bill of Rights, including the First Amendment.

tossups.p: This man secretly wrote resolutions passed by Virginia’s legislature in 1798 to protest the Alien and Sedition Acts, while his partner Thomas Jefferson wrote a similar set for Kentucky. The two men had founded the Democratic-Republican Party together.
tossups.r: This man later served as Jefferson’s Secretary of State. For 10 points, name this man who succeeded Jefferson as president.

tossups.p: At a 1790 dinner hosted by Thomas Jefferson, this congressman agreed to let Alexander Hamilton’s debt plan pass in exchange for placing the national capital on the Potomac River. The next year, he argued in Congress that Hamilton’s national bank was unconstitutional.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginia congressman who drafted the Bill of Rights and later became the fourth president.

tossups.p: This man, who graduated from the College of New Jersey, now Princeton, was the shortest president, at about five feet four inches tall. At college, he studied under John Witherspoon, a future signer of the Declaration of Independence. His portrait appeared on the $5,000 bill.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fourth president, the husband of Dolley and the main author of the Bill of Rights.

tossups.p: In 1809, this man reopened trade with Britain after its minister David Erskine promised that British limits on American shipping would end, but the British government rejected Erskine’s deal. Three years later, this president’s war message to Congress listed the impressment of American sailors among his complaints.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fourth president, who led the United States in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: This man was the last surviving signer of the Constitution when he died in 1836. Years earlier, he had joined Alexander Hamilton at the Annapolis Convention, which called for a larger meeting in Philadelphia to fix the Articles of Confederation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian known as the “Father of the Constitution,” who became the fourth president.

tossups.p: In 1810, Congress passed Macon’s Bill No. 2, and Napoleon then fooled this president into cutting off trade with Britain by pretending to drop France’s own limits on American ships. Later, New England Federalists who opposed this president’s war met at the Hartford Convention.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who asked Congress to declare war on Britain in 1812.

Known as the “Father of the Constitution”
Drafted the amendments that became the Bill of Rights and steered them through the First Congress (1789)

_Federalist_ No. 10: a large republic can control the dangers of “faction”
_Federalist_ No. 51: “If men were angels, no government would be necessary”; “ambition must be made to counteract ambition”
Founded the Democratic-Republican Party with Thomas Jefferson to oppose Alexander Hamilton’s Federalists
Secretly wrote the Virginia Resolutions (1798) against the Alien and Sedition Acts; Jefferson wrote Kentucky’s
Jefferson’s Secretary of State (1801–1809); William Marbury sued him over an undelivered commission

The shortest president, about 5 feet 4 inches tall
Proposed an amendment on congressional pay in 1789; it was finally ratified in 1992 as the 27th Amendment
Beat James Monroe in a 1789 House race after promising amendments, though he had once called lists of rights “parchment barriers”
His notes are the fullest record of the Constitutional Convention; they were published in 1840, after his death
The last surviving signer of the Constitution; died in 1836 and is buried at Montpelier, his Virginia home
Both vice presidents died in office: George Clinton (1812) and Elbridge Gerry (1814), the namesake of “gerrymander”
Just before leaving office (1817), vetoed John C. Calhoun’s Bonus Bill for roads and canals as unconstitutional
Opposed Hamilton’s national bank in 1791 but signed the charter of the Second Bank of the United States in 1816
Compromise of 1790: at Jefferson’s dinner, he let Hamilton’s debt plan pass in exchange for a capital on the Potomac
Lived in the Octagon House after the British burned the White House; signed the Treaty of Ghent into effect there (1815)

Attended the Annapolis Convention (1786) with Alexander Hamilton, which called for the Philadelphia convention

Graduated from the College of New Jersey (Princeton), where he studied under John Witherspoon; pictured on the $5,000 bill

trap.title: Madison, Jefferson, or Monroe?
trap.body: James Madison and Thomas Jefferson were close partners for about 50 years: they founded the Democratic-Republican Party, wrote the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, and Madison served as Jefferson’s Secretary of State before succeeding him. James Monroe, the next president, was a Virginia ally of both, so clues about one often name the others. _Marbury v. Madison_ is a trap too: it is a court case, so it is wrong when a question wants the man.
trap.fix: Madison clues: the Virginia Plan, _The Federalist Papers_ (Nos. 10 and 51), the Bill of Rights, the War of 1812, Dolley, and Montpelier. Jefferson clues: the Declaration, the Louisiana Purchase, and Monticello. Monroe clues: the Monroe Doctrine and the Era of Good Feelings. “Madison” alone is enough.

topics.name: Jefferson Davis
topics.kicker: President of the Confederacy · Former U.S. senator and Secretary of War
topics.briefing: Jefferson Davis was born in Kentucky in 1808, about eight months before Abraham Lincoln was born in the same state. He fought in the Mexican-American War, served as a U.S. senator from Mississippi and as Secretary of War, and in 1861 the seceded Southern states chose him as president of the Confederate States of America. After the South lost the Civil War, Union cavalry captured him in Georgia, and he spent two years in prison.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As Secretary of War, this man persuaded Congress to pay for importing camels so the army could test them for carrying supplies across the deserts of the Southwest. He also pushed for the Gadsden Purchase so a railroad to the Pacific could run through the South.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who served in Franklin Pierce’s cabinet before becoming president of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: This man’s first wife, Sarah Knox Taylor, died of malaria three months after their wedding, and her father, Zachary Taylor, had opposed the marriage. Years later, this man led the Mississippi Rifles under Taylor at the Battle of Buena Vista [“BWAY-nuh VEE-stuh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mississippian who became president of the Confederate States of America.

tossups.p: After two years as a prisoner at Fort Monroe in Virginia, this man was released on bail in 1867, with the newspaper editor Horace Greeley among those who signed his bond. He was charged with treason, but the government dropped the case without ever bringing him to trial.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who had served as the only president of the Confederate States of America.

tossups.p: Northern cartoonists mocked this man by drawing him escaping in a woman’s dress, an exaggeration of the fact that he had his wife Varina’s coat and shawl around him when soldiers of the 4th Michigan Cavalry caught him.
tossups.r: He was captured near Irwinville, Georgia, in May 1865. For 10 points, name this president of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: At Beauvoir [“bohv-WAHR”], his home on the Gulf Coast in Biloxi, Mississippi, this man wrote _The Rise and Fall of the Confederate Government_. He died in New Orleans in 1889 and was later reburied in Richmond, Virginia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who had been the president of the Confederacy during the Civil War.

tossups.p: In 1978, President Jimmy Carter signed a law restoring this man’s U.S. citizenship, almost 90 years after his death. Three years earlier, Congress had done the same for Robert E. Lee, the general this man had put in command of the Army of Northern Virginia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who led the Confederate States of America as its president from 1861 to 1865.

tossups.p: This leader often clashed with his own vice president, Alexander Stephens, who spent long stretches at home in Georgia criticizing policies such as the military draft. The two men had been chosen by delegates meeting in Montgomery, Alabama, in February 1861.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who served as president of the Confederate States of America.

tossups.p: When Joseph E. Johnston was wounded at the Battle of Seven Pines in 1862, this leader gave command of the army defending Richmond to his military adviser, Robert E. Lee. This leader also feuded with the general P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”].
tossups.r: Lee led that army, the Army of Northern Virginia, for the rest of the war. For 10 points, name this president of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: On a Sunday in April 1865, this man was handed a message from Robert E. Lee during services at St. Paul’s Church, warning that Richmond had to be abandoned. He and his cabinet fled south by train that night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president of the Confederacy, who was captured in Georgia the next month.

tossups.p: As a young army lieutenant, this man escorted the captured Sauk leader Black Hawk to prison in 1832. He was born in Kentucky in 1808, less than a year before his later rival, Abraham Lincoln, was born in the same state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who led the Confederate States of America during the Civil War.

tossups.p: In January 1861, this senator gave a farewell speech to the U.S. Senate, less than two weeks after his home state became the second to secede from the Union. He had earlier served as Secretary of War under Franklin Pierce.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mississippian who became president of the Confederate States of America.

tossups.p: Judah P. Benjamin, one of this man’s closest advisers, served in his cabinet as attorney general, secretary of war, and secretary of state. Benjamin escaped to England after this man’s government collapsed in 1865.
tossups.r: This man’s government had moved its capital to Richmond, Virginia, in 1861. For 10 points, name this president of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: This leader’s cabinet decided to fire on a fort in Charleston Harbor in April 1861, after Abraham Lincoln announced that he would send food to the soldiers there. General P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”] carried out the attack.
tossups.r: That attack on Fort Sumter began the Civil War. For 10 points, name this president of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: This man’s older brother Joseph helped him set up Brierfield, a cotton plantation on the Mississippi River that was worked by enslaved people. He had graduated from West Point in 1828 and served at army posts in what is now Wisconsin.
tossups.r: He later represented Mississippi in the U.S. Senate. For 10 points, name this man who became president of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: At the Battle of Buena Vista [“BWAY-nuh VEE-stuh”], this colonel’s Mississippi Rifles formed a V-shaped line to help turn back a Mexican cavalry charge, and he stayed in the fight even after being wounded. He had given up a seat in Congress to command that volunteer regiment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mississippian who later became president of the Confederate States of America.

U.S. senator from Mississippi who resigned when his state seceded in January 1861
His government’s capital moved from Montgomery, Alabama, to Richmond, Virginia, in 1861
Born in Kentucky in 1808, about eight months before Abraham Lincoln was born in the same state
Secretary of War under President Franklin Pierce (1853–1857)
Gave up a seat in Congress to lead the Mississippi Rifles in the Mexican-American War; wounded at Buena Vista (1847)
His vice president was Alexander Stephens of Georgia, with whom he often clashed
Gave Robert E. Lee command of the army defending Richmond, the Army of Northern Virginia (1862)
His government ordered the attack on Fort Sumter that began the Civil War (April 1861)
Fled Richmond in April 1865 and was captured by Union cavalry near Irwinville, Georgia, that May
Held prisoner at Fort Monroe, Virginia, for two years; charged with treason but never tried
Graduated from West Point (1828) and served at army posts on the frontier
As Secretary of War, brought camels to the U.S. Army to test them for carrying supplies in the Southwest
Pushed for the Gadsden Purchase (1853) so a southern railroad route could reach the Pacific
First wife, Sarah Knox Taylor, daughter of Zachary Taylor, died of malaria three months after their 1835 wedding

Released on bail in 1867; newspaper editor Horace Greeley helped sign his bail bond

trap.title: Jefferson, but not Thomas
trap.body: Jefferson Davis was named for Thomas Jefferson, so hearing “Jefferson” can tempt players to blurt out the third president, even though the two men came from different generations. Players also mix up the two Civil War presidents: Davis led the Confederacy from Richmond, while Abraham Lincoln led the Union from Washington. Robert E. Lee, Alexander Stephens, and Zachary Taylor show up in Davis clues as well.
trap.fix: Listen for the side and the era: “Confederate,” Richmond, Montgomery, Fort Monroe, Buena Vista, or camels in the army mean Davis. Thomas Jefferson clues come from the late 1700s and early 1800s: the Declaration, Monticello, and the Louisiana Purchase. “Davis” alone is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: Jefferson Davis (or Jefferson Finis Davis)

topics.name: John Quincy Adams
topics.kicker: 6th U.S. President · Son of John Adams and “Old Man Eloquent” in Congress
topics.briefing: John Quincy Adams watched the Battle of Bunker Hill from a hilltop when he was seven, and he spent the rest of his life serving his country. The son of John Adams, he helped end the War of 1812, wrote much of the Monroe Doctrine, and won a disputed election in 1824 to become the 6th president. After losing to Andrew Jackson, he served 17 years in the House of Representatives, where he fought a “gag rule” that blocked antislavery petitions.
topics.answerHtml: John Quincy Adams (or JQA; prompt on Adams; do not accept “John Adams”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his first annual message to Congress, this president called for a national university and astronomical observatories, which he called “lighthouses of the skies.” He also asked for federal spending on roads and canals and a naval academy, but critics mocked his plans.
tossups.r: He had won the presidency in the House of Representatives after the election of 1824. For 10 points, name this sixth president.

tossups.p: While serving as minister to Russia, this man turned down a seat on the Supreme Court after James Madison nominated him. Years earlier, at age 14, he had traveled to St. Petersburg as a secretary for the American diplomat Francis Dana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this son of John and Abigail Adams who became the sixth president of the United States.

tossups.p: As a seven-year-old, this future president watched the Battle of Bunker Hill from a hilltop with his mother. He later taught rhetoric and oratory as a professor at Harvard while also serving as a U.S. senator.
tossups.r: He was the first president whose father had also been president. For 10 points, name this sixth president.

tossups.p: In 1841, this former president argued before the Supreme Court on behalf of Africans who had taken over the Spanish ship _La Amistad_, and the Court ruled that they should go free. Anthony Hopkins played him in a 1997 Steven Spielberg film about the case.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sixth president, who served in Congress after leaving the White House.

tossups.p: For eight years, this congressman fought the “gag rule,” which automatically tabled antislavery petitions sent to the House, until it was finally repealed in 1844. His speeches in Congress earned him the nickname “Old Man Eloquent.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former president who served in the House after leaving the White House.

tossups.p: This congressman collapsed at his desk in the House of Representatives in 1848 and died two days later in the Capitol, reportedly saying, “This is the last of earth. I am content.” A young Illinois congressman named Abraham Lincoln was serving in the House at the time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who had been the sixth president, the son of the second.

tossups.p: In a four-way presidential race that also included William Crawford and Henry Clay, this man finished second in both popular and electoral votes, but no candidate won a majority of electoral votes. Under the Twelfth Amendment, the House had to choose among the top three finishers, which left Clay out.
tossups.r: The House chose this man over Andrew Jackson, who called the result a “corrupt bargain.” For 10 points, name this winner of the election of 1824.

tossups.p: As Secretary of State, this man convinced James Monroe to issue a warning to Europe on America’s own, rather than jointly with Britain, as British foreign secretary George Canning had proposed. He held that cabinet job through nearly all of Monroe’s two terms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who wrote much of the Monroe Doctrine and later became the sixth president.

tossups.p: This diplomat negotiated the Transcontinental Treaty with Spain’s minister Luis de Onís [“oh-NEES”], which gave Florida to the United States and drew a border with Spanish lands all the way to the Pacific. He also defended Andrew Jackson’s invasion of Florida when other cabinet members wanted Jackson punished.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Secretary of State under James Monroe who later became the sixth president.

tossups.p: This diplomat led the American team, which also included Henry Clay and Albert Gallatin, that negotiated a Christmas Eve treaty in what is now Belgium. He later served as minister to Great Britain, a post his father had held.
tossups.r: That treaty ended the War of 1812. For 10 points, name this son of the second president who became the sixth president.

tossups.p: Southerners called a tariff this president signed in 1828 the “Tariff of Abominations,” and his own vice president, John C. Calhoun, secretly wrote a protest against it. That protest was called the “South Carolina Exposition and Protest.”
tossups.r: Later that year, this president lost his bid for reelection to Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this sixth president.

tossups.p: This congressman led a long fight to make sure that money left to the United States by the British scientist James Smithson was used, as Smithson’s will asked, for “the increase and diffusion of knowledge.” Some members of Congress had wanted to refuse the gift.
tossups.r: That gift founded the Smithsonian Institution. For 10 points, name this former president who later served in the House.

tossups.p: This president’s wife, Louisa Catherine, was born in London, making her the first First Lady born outside the United States. He refused to attend the inauguration of the man who defeated him.
tossups.r: His father had done the same in 1801. For 10 points, name this sixth president, the son of John and Abigail Adams.

tossups.p: Elected to the Senate as a Federalist from Massachusetts, this man angered his party by supporting Thomas Jefferson’s Embargo Act, and he resigned his seat in 1808. He had earlier served as minister to the Netherlands and to Prussia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who later became the sixth president, following in his father’s footsteps.

tossups.p: This president often began his day with a swim in the Potomac River, and the diary he kept for more than sixty years is a famous record of early American politics. He is buried in a Massachusetts church nicknamed the “Church of the Presidents.”
tossups.r: His parents are buried there too. For 10 points, name this sixth president, the son of John Adams.

Son of John Adams, the 2nd president, and Abigail Adams
Won the election of 1824 in the House; Andrew Jackson called it a “corrupt bargain” with Henry Clay

Served 17 years in the House of Representatives after his presidency (1831–1848)
Nicknamed “Old Man Eloquent” for his speeches in Congress
Collapsed at his desk in the House in 1848 and died two days later: “This is the last of earth. I am content.”
Led the Americans who negotiated the Treaty of Ghent (1814), ending the War of 1812
Signed the Tariff of 1828, which Southerners called the “Tariff of Abominations”
As a seven-year-old, watched the Battle of Bunker Hill (1775) with his mother
His first annual message (1825) asked for a national university and observatories, “lighthouses of the skies”
At 14, went to Russia as secretary to diplomat Francis Dana; later U.S. minister to Russia
Turned down a seat on the Supreme Court after James Madison nominated him (1811)
Negotiated the Transcontinental Treaty with Spain’s Luis de Onís (1819), which gave Florida to the United States
In Monroe’s cabinet, defended Andrew Jackson’s 1818 invasion of Spanish Florida
In 1824, the 12th Amendment sent the race to the House, which chose among the top three; fourth-place Henry Clay was left out
Fought to use James Smithson’s gift for its intended purpose, founding the Smithsonian Institution
Taught rhetoric and oratory as a Harvard professor while also serving in the Senate

Played by Anthony Hopkins in Steven Spielberg’s film _Amistad_ (1997)

Minister to the Netherlands (named by Washington) and Prussia (named by his father); later minister to Great Britain

trap.title: Father or son?
trap.body: John Quincy Adams (6th president) and his father, John Adams (2nd president), were both Massachusetts diplomats who served one term as president and skipped the next president’s inauguration. Real answer lines say “do not accept John Adams,” so leaving out “Quincy” loses the tossup, and saying only “Adams” earns just a prompt. Samuel Adams, John Adams’s cousin, is a third Adams to avoid.
trap.fix: Son clues: the Treaty of Ghent, the Monroe Doctrine, the “corrupt bargain” of 1824, the Tariff of Abominations, the gag rule, the Amistad case, and dying in the Capitol in 1848. Father clues: the Boston Massacre trial, the XYZ Affair, the Alien and Sedition Acts, and dying on July 4, 1826. When prompted, say “John Quincy Adams.”
trap.line: Real answer line: John Quincy Adams (or JQA; prompt on Adams; do not accept or prompt on “John Adams”)

topics.name: John Wilkes Booth
topics.kicker: Actor and Confederate sympathizer · Assassinated Abraham Lincoln in 1865
topics.briefing: John Wilkes Booth was one of the most popular actors in America, the son and brother of famous Shakespearean actors, and he strongly supported the Confederacy. On April 14, 1865, five days after Robert E. Lee surrendered, Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C. Union soldiers tracked him to a Virginia farm 12 days later, where he was shot and killed.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man knew the play being performed that night so well that he timed his attack to a big laugh, when a character was called a “sockdologizing old man-trap.” He then leaped from the presidential box to the stage and broke his leg.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this actor and Confederate sympathizer who shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre.

tossups.p: Twelve days after his most famous act, this man was trapped in a tobacco barn on Richard Garrett’s farm in Virginia, where Sergeant Boston Corbett shot him against orders. His last words were reportedly “Useless, useless.”
tossups.r: His companion, David Herold, had surrendered. For 10 points, name this man who had assassinated President Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: After breaking his leg, this man rode to the Maryland home of Dr. Samuel Mudd, who set the leg, and Mudd was later sent to prison for helping him. On the way, he had stopped at a tavern owned by Mary Surratt to pick up supplies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Confederate sympathizer and actor who shot President Abraham Lincoln in April 1865.

tossups.p: This man’s older brother Edwin, the most celebrated Hamlet of his time, once pulled Abraham Lincoln’s son Robert to safety when he slipped beside a moving train. Their father, Junius Brutus, had come to America from England.
tossups.r: In 1865, this man shot the president at Ford’s Theatre. For 10 points, name this actor, a supporter of the Confederacy.

tossups.p: In November 1864, this man played Mark Antony in a one-night benefit performance of _Julius Caesar_ in New York, while his brothers Edwin and Junius Jr. played Brutus and Cassius. The show raised money for a statue of William Shakespeare in Central Park.
tossups.r: Less than five months later, this actor shot a president. For 10 points, name this man who killed Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: In 1859, this man joined a Virginia militia company so that he could watch the execution of the abolitionist John Brown in Charles Town. Though he never served as a soldier in the Civil War, he became a passionate supporter of the Confederacy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this actor who shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in April 1865.

tossups.p: A photograph of Abraham Lincoln’s second inauguration in March 1865 shows this man in the crowd at the Capitol. That same month, his plan to kidnap Lincoln and trade him for Confederate prisoners fell apart when the president changed his plans.
tossups.r: Weeks later, this man shot Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre. For 10 points, name this assassin.

tossups.p: This man assigned George Atzerodt to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson at the Kirkwood House hotel, but Atzerodt lost his nerve and never made the attempt. On the same night, Lewis Powell attacked Secretary of State William Seward at his home.
tossups.r: Seward survived. For 10 points, name this leader of the plot, who shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre.

tossups.p: Plotters met with this man at a Washington boarding house run by Mary Surratt, who became the first woman executed by the federal government. She and seven other people accused of helping him were tried by a military commission.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865.

tossups.p: After his crime, this man shouted the Latin words “Sic semper tyrannis” [“sik SEM-per tih-RAN-iss”], Virginia’s state motto, which means “thus always to tyrants.” Major Henry Rathbone, who was sitting nearby with his fiancée, Clara Harris, tried to stop him and was wounded.
tossups.r: Lincoln had been watching _Our American Cousin_. For 10 points, name this assassin of President Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: For several days, this man and David Herold hid in a pine thicket in southern Maryland, where Thomas Jones brought them food and newspapers. Jones then gave them a boat so they could cross the Potomac River into Virginia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who was hunted by Union soldiers after he shot Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: Standing in the crowd outside the White House on April 11, 1865, this man heard Abraham Lincoln support voting rights for some Black men, and he reportedly vowed that it would be the last speech Lincoln ever gave. Lewis Powell was with him.
tossups.r: Three days later, he shot Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre. For 10 points, name this actor.

tossups.p: On a Friday morning in April 1865, this man stopped at a theater to pick up his mail and learned that the president planned to attend a play there that night. General Ulysses S. Grant had been invited too, but he and his wife later backed out.
tossups.r: The Lincolns brought Henry Rathbone and Clara Harris instead. For 10 points, name this actor who shot Abraham Lincoln in that theater.

tossups.p: While hiding from soldiers, this man wrote in a pocket diary that he was being hunted for doing what Brutus had been honored for. He also compared himself to William Tell. A War Department poster offered fifty thousand dollars for his capture.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who was tracked down twelve days after shooting Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: This man, born near Bel Air, Maryland, is buried in an unmarked grave at Green Mount Cemetery in Baltimore. The government first buried him secretly at an army arsenal in Washington and released his body to his family in 1869.
tossups.r: Before 1865, he was one of the most popular actors in America. For 10 points, name this man who shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre.

Hid in a Maryland pine thicket, where Thomas Jones brought food and newspapers, then crossed the Potomac by boat
