trap.title: Assassin, victim, or event?
trap.body: The same clues, like Ford’s Theatre, _Our American Cousin_, Mary Surratt, and Dr. Samuel Mudd, show up in three answer lines: John Wilkes Booth (the assassin), Abraham Lincoln (the president he shot), and the assassination of Abraham Lincoln (the event). Answering “Lincoln” to a question about the killer is wrong. Booth’s brother Edwin was a famous actor too, so “Edwin Booth” is a trap.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this actor” or “this assassin” wants John Wilkes Booth, “this president” wants Lincoln, and “this event” wants the assassination of Abraham Lincoln. Hamlet and saving Robert Lincoln from a train point to Edwin. Saying “John Wilkes Booth” in full is safest.
trap.line: Real answer line: John Wilkes Booth (do not accept “Edwin Booth”)

topics.name: Louisiana Purchase
topics.kicker: 1803 land deal with Napoleon’s France · Doubled the size of the U.S.
topics.briefing: In 1803, American diplomats in Paris were trying to buy the port city of New Orleans when France offered them the entire Louisiana Territory instead. For $15 million, the United States roughly doubled in size, gaining land that became all or part of 15 states. President Thomas Jefferson worried the Constitution didn’t allow such a purchase, but he made the deal anyway and sent Lewis and Clark to explore it.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Robert Livingston was startled when the French foreign minister, Talleyrand [“TAL-ee-rand”], asked how much the United States would pay for “the whole” of a vast territory instead of just one city. Livingston and James Monroe then signed a treaty with François Barbé-Marbois [“bar-BAY mar-BWAH”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 land deal that doubled the size of the United States.

tossups.p: Thousands of French soldiers under Charles Leclerc [“luh-KLAIR”] died of yellow fever and in battle while trying to retake the colony of Saint-Domingue [“san doh-MANG”], which led the French government to give up its plans for an empire in North America. This deal soon followed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 land deal in which Napoleon sold a huge territory to the United States.

tossups.p: A Spanish official took away the American “right of deposit,” which let farmers store goods at a port near the mouth of the Mississippi River. The president then sent James Monroe to France with orders to buy that port, but the diplomats came home with much more.
tossups.r: That port was New Orleans. For 10 points, name this 1803 deal that doubled the size of the United States.

tossups.p: In an 1802 letter, the president who made this deal warned that “there is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy,” meaning the port of New Orleans.
tossups.r: A year later, his diplomats bought that port and a huge region around it. For 10 points, name this land deal with Napoleon’s France.

tossups.p: Because he believed the federal government had only the powers the Constitution listed, the president who made this deal drafted an amendment to allow it, but he dropped the idea for fear that the seller would change its mind. New England Federalists argued against it in the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 land deal in which the United States paid France 15 million dollars.

tossups.p: The United States paid for this deal with bonds that were bought and resold by Baring Brothers, a British bank, and Hope and Company, a Dutch bank, even though Britain and France were about to go back to war. France used the money to prepare for that war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 deal in which the United States bought a vast territory west of the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: On “Three Flags Day” in March 1804, the flag of Spain was lowered in St. Louis, the French flag flew briefly, and then the American flag was raised to complete this deal. The formal handover in New Orleans had taken place the previous December.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this land deal in which Thomas Jefferson bought a vast territory from Napoleon in 1803.

tossups.p: The 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis, where the Summer Olympics were also held, celebrated the 100th anniversary of this event. The Gateway Arch in St. Louis also honors this event and the westward expansion that followed it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 deal in which the United States bought a huge territory from France.

tossups.p: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 banned slavery north of the 36°30′ line in the rest of the land gained in this deal, a ban that the Kansas–Nebraska Act later overturned. Zebulon Pike explored the southwestern part of that land.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this deal, explored by Lewis and Clark, that doubled the size of the United States in 1803.

tossups.p: In the secret Treaty of San Ildefonso [“san eel-day-FOHN-soh”] in 1800, Spain handed a huge North American territory back to France, which alarmed Americans who shipped their crops down the Mississippi River. Spain had controlled that territory since the end of the French and Indian War.
tossups.r: Three years later, France sold that territory to the United States. For 10 points, name this deal arranged by Thomas Jefferson’s diplomats.

tossups.p: After signing this agreement, Robert Livingston reportedly declared, “We have lived long, but this is the noblest work of our whole lives.” Livingston had been joined in Paris by James Monroe, who was sent as a special envoy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 deal in which the United States bought a vast territory from Napoleon’s France.

tossups.p: Land gained in this deal makes up all or part of fifteen states, including Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Montana, and it covered about 828,000 square miles. Its southern part became the Territory of Orleans, which joined the Union as a state in 1812.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 deal that doubled the size of the United States for 15 million dollars.

tossups.p: This deal transferred a region that the French explorer La Salle [“luh SAL”] had claimed in 1682 and named in honor of King Louis XIV. It covered most of the land drained by the Mississippi River’s western branches, reaching to the Rocky Mountains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 deal in which Thomas Jefferson bought that vast territory from France.

tossups.p: Because the treaty for this deal described its borders only vaguely, the United States and Spain argued over them until the Transcontinental Treaty of 1819 settled the boundary. The United States also claimed that this deal included West Florida, which Spain denied.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 land deal whose lands were explored by Lewis and Clark.

tossups.p: Needing money for a coming war with Britain, the ruler who made this deal with the United States reportedly predicted that it would give Britain a rival at sea that would one day humble its pride. He had once hoped to use this land to feed his sugar colonies in the Caribbean.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1803 deal in which Napoleon sold a vast territory to the United States.

clues.t: Made in 1803 by President Thomas Jefferson
Bought from Napoleon’s France for $15 million
Doubled the size of the United States, adding about 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi River
Explored by Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery (1804–1806)
Included the port of New Orleans, which American diplomats had first been sent to buy by itself
Negotiated in Paris by Robert Livingston and James Monroe
France gave up on an American empire after its army failed to retake Saint-Domingue (Haiti)
Jefferson, a strict constructionist, worried the Constitution did not allow buying land and considered an amendment
Its land became all or part of 15 states, including Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Montana
Spain took away the American “right of deposit” at New Orleans in 1802, alarming Western farmers
Spain had secretly given the territory back to France in the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800)
French foreign minister Talleyrand surprised Livingston by asking what the U.S. would pay for “the whole”
The Missouri Compromise (1820) banned slavery in its land north of 36°30′, until the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854)
Many New England Federalists opposed it, fearing new western states would weaken their region
François Barbé-Marbois signed the treaty for France
Paid for with bonds handled by Baring Brothers of Britain and Hope and Company of the Netherlands
“Three Flags Day” (March 1804): the Spanish, French, and American flags flew in turn over St. Louis
The 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis celebrated its 100th anniversary
Jefferson wrote (1802) that whoever held New Orleans was “our natural and habitual enemy”
Its unclear borders with Spanish land were settled by the Transcontinental Treaty (1819); the U.S. also claimed West Florida
Its southern part became the Territory of Orleans, which became a state in 1812
La Salle claimed the region for France in 1682, naming it for King Louis XIV
The Gateway Arch in St. Louis honors it and the westward expansion that followed
Zebulon Pike explored its southwestern part (1806–1807)
Livingston reportedly said: “We have lived long, but this is the noblest work of our whole lives”
Napoleon needed money for a new war with Britain and had once hoped the land would feed his Caribbean sugar colonies
Thousands of French soldiers under Charles Leclerc died of yellow fever and in battle in Saint-Domingue

trap.title: Deal, land, or state?
trap.body: The Louisiana Purchase was the 1803 deal; the land itself is often called the Louisiana Territory, and the modern state of Louisiana is only a small corner of it. Saying just “Louisiana” earns a prompt. Players also mix it up with other land deals: the Gadsden Purchase (1853, from Mexico), the Alaska Purchase (1867, from Russia), and the Mexican Cession (1848, after a war).
trap.fix: Napoleon, Jefferson, Livingston and Monroe, New Orleans, Saint-Domingue, and Lewis and Clark all mean the Louisiana Purchase. A southern railroad route means Gadsden, and “Seward’s Folly” means Alaska. When you get a prompt, say “Louisiana Purchase.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Louisiana Purchase (prompt on Louisiana or Louisiana Territory)

topics.name: Lyndon B. Johnson
topics.kicker: 36th U.S. President · The Great Society, civil rights laws, and Vietnam
topics.briefing: Lyndon B. Johnson grew up in the Texas Hill Country, taught Mexican American children in a small Texas town, and rose to become Senate Majority Leader. When John F. Kennedy was assassinated in 1963, Johnson was sworn in as president aboard Air Force One. As the 36th president, he signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act and launched the Great Society, while the number of U.S. troops in the Vietnam War grew to more than 500,000.
topics.answerHtml: Lyndon Baines Johnson (or LBJ; prompt on Johnson; do not accept “Andrew Johnson”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young man, this future president taught Mexican American children at a poor school in Cotulla, Texas, and decades later he described those students in a speech to Congress asking for a voting rights law. That 1965 speech included the words “we shall overcome.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who signed the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

tossups.p: This man beat former Texas governor Coke Stevenson by just 87 votes in a disputed 1948 runoff for a Senate nomination, earning a joking nickname that called his win a “landslide.” He later became Senate Majority Leader.
tossups.r: NASA’s space center in Houston, home of Mission Control, is named for him. For 10 points, name this Texan who became president after John F. Kennedy was assassinated.

tossups.p: A week after taking office, this president created a commission led by Chief Justice Earl Warren to investigate the killing of the man he had replaced. He had been sworn in aboard Air Force One by Judge Sarah T. Hughes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vice president who became president when John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas.

tossups.p: After reports that North Vietnamese boats had attacked American destroyers in August 1964, Congress passed a resolution giving this president broad power to use military force in Southeast Asia. He then began Operation Rolling Thunder, a long bombing campaign against North Vietnam.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who greatly expanded U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War.

tossups.p: A 1964 campaign ad for this candidate showed a little girl counting as she picked petals off a daisy before the screen filled with a nuclear explosion; it aired only once as a paid ad. He won that election in a landslide over Barry Goldwater.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who had taken office the year before, after John F. Kennedy’s assassination.

tossups.p: On March 31, 1968, this president surprised the nation in a televised speech by saying, “I shall not seek, and I will not accept, the nomination of my party for another term.” Weeks earlier, Eugene McCarthy had done surprisingly well against him in the New Hampshire primary.
tossups.r: His vice president, Hubert Humphrey, won the Democratic nomination but lost to Richard Nixon. For 10 points, name this president.

tossups.p: This president signed a 1965 health insurance law at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, and handed former president Harry Truman the first card issued under the new program. That law created Medicare and Medicaid.
tossups.r: His wife, Lady Bird, led a campaign to beautify America’s highways. For 10 points, name this president whose programs were called the Great Society.

tossups.p: After riots broke out in Detroit, Newark, and other cities in 1967, this president created the Kerner Commission, which warned that the nation was “moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal.” Its official name was the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders.
tossups.r: He had earlier signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964. For 10 points, name this 36th president.

tossups.p: This president named Robert Weaver to lead the new Department of Housing and Urban Development, making him the first African American cabinet secretary. A year later, this president appointed Thurgood Marshall as the first African American Supreme Court justice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Texan who launched the Great Society after succeeding John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: At the foot of the Statue of Liberty in 1965, this president signed the Hart–Celler Act, which ended immigration quotas based on national origin that had favored immigrants from northern and western Europe. That same year, he signed a law creating the National Endowment for the Arts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Texan who signed both the Voting Rights Act and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

tossups.p: In his first State of the Union address, in January 1964, this president declared “unconditional war on poverty in America.” Programs that followed included Head Start for preschoolers and the Job Corps for young workers.
tossups.r: Months later, at the University of Michigan, he described his goals as the “Great Society.” For 10 points, name this president.

tossups.p: In 1967, this president met Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin [“kuh-SEE-gin”] for a summit at a small college in Glassboro, New Jersey. Two years earlier, he had sent U.S. Marines to the Dominican Republic during a civil war there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who expanded American involvement in the Vietnam War.

tossups.p: Robert Caro won a Pulitzer Prize for _Master of the Senate_, one volume of his giant biography of this man. Bryan Cranston won a Tony Award for playing this man in _All the Way_, a play about his first year as president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 after succeeding John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: As Senate Majority Leader, this man pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1957, and senators described being cornered by his famous “Treatment,” in which he leaned in close and argued until they agreed. He suffered a serious heart attack in 1955 but soon returned to lead the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Texan who served as John F. Kennedy’s vice president and then as president.

tossups.p: This president signed the Elementary and Secondary Education Act in front of the one-room schoolhouse he had attended as a boy, with his first teacher at his side. He died at his ranch on the Pedernales [“pur-dn-AL-iss”] River in January 1973, days before a peace agreement on Vietnam was signed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 36th president, a Texas Democrat whose wife was known as Lady Bird.

clues.t: 36th President (1963–1969), a Democrat from Texas
Became president when John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas (November 22, 1963); he had been Kennedy’s vice president
Called his domestic programs the “Great Society”
Signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965
Greatly expanded U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War; American troops there grew to more than 500,000
Sworn in aboard Air Force One by Judge Sarah T. Hughes, with Jacqueline Kennedy beside him
The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) gave him broad war powers; Operation Rolling Thunder bombed North Vietnam (1965–1968)
Declared an “unconditional war on poverty” (1964); programs included Head Start and the Job Corps
Signed Medicare and Medicaid (1965) at Harry Truman’s library and gave Truman the first Medicare card
Beat Barry Goldwater in a 1964 landslide; his campaign’s “Daisy” ad warned of nuclear war
On March 31, 1968, announced, “I shall not seek, and I will not accept” his party’s nomination for another term
Appointed Thurgood Marshall, the first African American Supreme Court justice (1967)
His wife, Lady Bird, led a campaign to beautify America’s highways
Created the Warren Commission, led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, to investigate Kennedy’s assassination
Senate Majority Leader in the 1950s, famous for “the Treatment”; pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1957
Taught Mexican American children in Cotulla, Texas, and recalled them in his 1965 voting rights speech
Won a disputed 1948 Senate runoff over Coke Stevenson by just 87 votes, earning a joking nickname about his “landslide”
His 1965 voting rights speech to Congress included the civil rights anthem’s words “we shall overcome”
Signed the Hart–Celler Act (1965) at the Statue of Liberty, ending immigration quotas based on national origin
His Kerner Commission’s 1968 report warned the nation was “moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal”
Met Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin at Glassboro, New Jersey (1967); sent Marines to the Dominican Republic (1965)
Robert Caro’s biography volume _Master of the Senate_ won a Pulitzer; Bryan Cranston played him in the play _All the Way_
Created the Department of Housing and Urban Development (1965); Robert Weaver became the first African American cabinet secretary
Signed the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965) outside his boyhood one-room school, beside his first teacher
Died at his ranch on the Pedernales River in January 1973, days before the Vietnam peace agreement was signed
Eugene McCarthy did well against him in New Hampshire (1968); his vice president, Hubert Humphrey, then lost to Richard Nixon
NASA’s space center in Houston, home of Mission Control, is named for him

trap.title: Which President Johnson?
trap.body: Two presidents named Johnson took office after an assassination: Andrew Johnson replaced Abraham Lincoln in 1865, and Lyndon B. Johnson replaced John F. Kennedy in 1963. Real LBJ answer lines say “do not accept or prompt on Andrew Johnson,” and saying just “Johnson” earns only a prompt. Vietnam clues are another trap: Johnson escalated the war after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, while Richard Nixon slowly brought troops home through “Vietnamization.”
trap.fix: Civil rights laws, the Great Society, Medicare, Air Force One, and the Gulf of Tonkin mean Lyndon Johnson; Reconstruction, the Tenure of Office Act, and impeachment in 1868 mean Andrew Johnson. When the moderator prompts, say “Lyndon Johnson” or “LBJ.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Lyndon Baines Johnson (or LBJ; prompt on Johnson; do not accept or prompt on “Andrew Johnson”)

topics.name: Manhattan Project
topics.kicker: Secret U.S. program in World War II · Built the first atomic bombs
topics.briefing: In 1942, the U.S. Army launched a top-secret program to build an atomic bomb before Nazi Germany could. General Leslie Groves ran it, J. Robert Oppenheimer directed its hidden laboratory at Los Alamos, New Mexico, and huge secret plants rose at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and Hanford, Washington. Its first bomb was tested in the New Mexico desert on July 16, 1945, and weeks later the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan.
topics.answerHtml: Manhattan Project (accept Manhattan Engineer District; prompt on descriptions like “building the atomic bomb”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Economist Alexander Sachs personally delivered a letter to the president in October 1939 warning that “extremely powerful bombs of a new type” might be built using uranium. Leo Szilard [“SIL-ard”] drafted that letter and Albert Einstein signed it, leading to a small Advisory Committee on Uranium that was the first step toward this program.
tossups.r: J. Robert Oppenheimer later directed its laboratory at Los Alamos. For 10 points, name this secret World War II program that built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: After a test beneath the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, Arthur Compton told James Conant in a coded phone call that “the Italian navigator has landed in the New World.” That December 2, 1942, test, run by Enrico Fermi’s team in a reactor called Chicago Pile-1, achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret wartime program, led by General Leslie Groves, that built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: Before taking charge of this program in September 1942, Army engineer Leslie Groves had overseen construction of the Pentagon. Within days, Groves approved buying land for secret plants in Tennessee, and he later chose a Berkeley physicist who had never run a large project to lead its weapons laboratory in New Mexico.
tossups.r: That physicist was J. Robert Oppenheimer. For 10 points, name this World War II program that built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: At the K-25 plant in this program’s “secret city” in Tennessee, uranium hexafluoride gas was pumped through thousands of porous barriers to separate uranium-235. Nearby, at the Y-12 plant, Ernest Lawrence’s calutrons [“KAL-yoo-trons”] did the same job with giant magnets wound with silver borrowed from the U.S. Treasury.
tossups.r: That city was Oak Ridge. For 10 points, name this World War II project, whose uranium bomb was dropped on Hiroshima.

tossups.p: This program built the B Reactor beside the Columbia River, where workers began producing plutonium in late 1944. That remote site in Washington state was chosen partly because the river could supply huge amounts of cold water to cool the reactors.
tossups.r: That site was Hanford. Its plutonium went into the bomb dropped on Nagasaki. For 10 points, name this secret project that built the first atomic weapons.

tossups.p: Enrico Fermi estimated the strength of a blast by dropping scraps of paper and watching how far they moved during this program’s test of a device nicknamed “the Gadget.” That July 16, 1945, explosion in the Jornada del Muerto [“hor-NAH-dah del MWAIR-toh”] desert of New Mexico melted sand into a green glass later called trinitite.
tossups.r: That test was code-named Trinity. For 10 points, name this secret program that built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: After watching this program’s first test, its laboratory director remembered a line from the Hindu scripture the _Bhagavad Gita_ [“BAH-guh-vahd GEE-tah”]: “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.” That director later linked the test’s code name, Trinity, to poems by John Donne.
tossups.r: That director, J. Robert Oppenheimer, led the lab at Los Alamos. For 10 points, name this World War II program that built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: Scientists in this program abandoned a simple “gun-type” design for plutonium and instead built an implosion weapon, which squeezed a plutonium core with carefully shaped explosives. Its uranium bomb, nicknamed “Little Boy,” used the simpler gun-type design and was never tested before it was used.
tossups.r: The plutonium bomb was called “Fat Man.” For 10 points, name this program whose bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

tossups.p: Colonel Paul Tibbets named his B-29 bomber after his mother before flying a mission from the island of Tinian. Three days later, Major Charles Sweeney, flying _Bockscar_, turned away from his first target, Kokura, because clouds and smoke hid the city.
tossups.r: Those planes, including the _Enola Gay_, dropped this program’s bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. For 10 points, name this secret U.S. project of World War II.

tossups.p: German-born physicist Klaus Fuchs [“FOOKS”] secretly passed details of this program’s work to the Soviet Union, and so did David Greenglass, an Army machinist at its New Mexico laboratory. Greenglass later testified against his sister and her husband, Ethel and Julius Rosenberg, who were convicted of spying and executed in 1953.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this World War II program that built atomic bombs at Los Alamos with materials from Oak Ridge and Hanford.

tossups.p: Mail for scientists at this program’s most secret laboratory went to a single address, P.O. Box 1663 in Santa Fe. The Army built that laboratory on a New Mexico mesa after buying out a private ranch school for boys.
tossups.r: This program’s name came from an Army Corps of Engineers district first based in New York City. For 10 points, name this project that built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: Secretary of War Henry Stimson briefed a new president about this program only after Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, because that man had not been told about it as vice president. That July, the new president learned of this program’s successful test while he was at the Potsdam Conference.
tossups.r: That president, Harry Truman, approved using its bombs against Japan. For 10 points, name this secret World War II program.

tossups.p: In July 1945, dozens of this program’s scientists signed a petition written by Leo Szilard [“SIL-ard”] asking the president not to use its new weapon against Japan without first giving Japan a chance to surrender. A month earlier, a report led by James Franck had suggested first showing the weapon’s power in an uninhabited area.
tossups.r: Its first test was code-named Trinity. For 10 points, name this secret program that built the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

tossups.p: The Danish physicist Niels Bohr visited this program’s main laboratory under the false name “Nicholas Baker,” and a young Richard Feynman amused himself there by cracking open his co-workers’ safes. Edward Teller spent much of his time at that laboratory working on ideas for a far more powerful weapon nicknamed “the Super.”
tossups.r: That laboratory was at Los Alamos. For 10 points, name this World War II program whose scientists built the first atomic bombs.

tossups.p: Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, a civilian commission took over this program’s work on January 1, 1947. A national historical park created in 2015 connects its three main sites in New Mexico, Tennessee, and Washington state, and a 2023 film about the director of its weapons laboratory won Best Picture.
tossups.r: That film is Christopher Nolan’s _Oppenheimer_. For 10 points, name this secret World War II program that built the first atomic bombs.

clues.t: Secret U.S. program in World War II (1942–1947) that built the first atomic bombs
J. Robert Oppenheimer directed its weapons laboratory and is called the “father of the atomic bomb”
Its bombs were dropped on Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9, 1945), the only nuclear weapons ever used in war
Its bombs were designed at a secret laboratory at Los Alamos, New Mexico, which opened in 1943
Army engineer General Leslie Groves ran it from September 1942; he had overseen building the Pentagon
A 1939 letter drafted by Leo Szilard and signed by Albert Einstein warned Franklin Roosevelt that Germany might build a uranium bomb
The Trinity test (July 16, 1945) in the New Mexico desert was the first nuclear explosion
Enrico Fermi’s team built Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor, and ran the first self-sustaining chain reaction on December 2, 1942
Oak Ridge, Tennessee, a “secret city,” enriched uranium-235 at plants like K-25 and Y-12
Hanford, Washington, on the Columbia River, made plutonium in reactors like the B Reactor
“Little Boy” (uranium, gun-type, never tested first) hit Hiroshima; “Fat Man” (plutonium, implosion) hit Nagasaki
Harry Truman, told about it only after Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, approved using its bombs on Japan
Named for an Army Corps of Engineers district whose first offices were in New York City
Economist Alexander Sachs delivered the Einstein–Szilard letter in October 1939; it led to the Advisory Committee on Uranium
Arthur Compton’s coded message: “The Italian navigator has landed in the New World”; the reactor sat under Stagg Field’s stands
K-25 used gaseous diffusion; Y-12 used Ernest Lawrence’s calutrons, built with silver borrowed from the Treasury
The Trinity device was nicknamed “the Gadget”; the blast in the Jornada del Muerto made green trinitite, and Fermi measured it with paper scraps
Oppenheimer recalled the _Bhagavad Gita_: “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds”; he linked “Trinity” to John Donne’s poems
The B-29 _Enola Gay_, named for pilot Paul Tibbets’s mother, flew from Tinian; _Bockscar_ (Charles Sweeney) turned away from cloudy Kokura
Klaus Fuchs and David Greenglass passed its secrets to the Soviet Union; Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in 1953
Mail to the Los Alamos lab went to P.O. Box 1663 in Santa Fe; the Army had bought out a boys’ ranch school there
Secretary of War Henry Stimson briefed Truman, who heard of the successful test at the Potsdam Conference (July 1945)
The Franck Report (June 1945) and Leo Szilard’s petition (July 1945) urged warning Japan or showing the bomb’s power before using it
Niels Bohr visited Los Alamos as “Nicholas Baker”; Richard Feynman cracked safes there; Edward Teller worked on “the Super”
The Atomic Energy Commission took over its work on January 1, 1947; a 2015 national historical park links its three main sites
Christopher Nolan’s film _Oppenheimer_ (2023), about its laboratory director, won Best Picture

trap.title: Program, place, or person?
trap.body: Many clues for this answer name a place (Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Hanford), a test (Trinity), a bomb (Little Boy or Fat Man), or a person (Oppenheimer, Groves, Fermi, Einstein). Each of those can be an answer line of its own, and Oppenheimer and Fermi are separate topics on this site. If the question asks for “this program” or “this project,” none of them is right: the answer is the whole effort.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this program” or “this project” means the Manhattan Project; “this test” means Trinity; “this laboratory” or “this town” means Los Alamos; “this physicist” or “this general” means a person. Saying only “the atomic bomb” earns a prompt, so be ready to say “Manhattan Project.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Manhattan Project (accept Manhattan Engineer District; prompt on descriptions like “building the atomic bomb”)

topics.name: Pennsylvania
topics.kicker: The Keystone State · William Penn’s Quaker colony
topics.briefing: In 1681, King Charles II paid off a debt he had owed to a late admiral by giving the admiral’s son, William Penn, a huge American colony, named “Penn’s Woods” in the father’s honor. Penn, a Quaker, made it a “Holy Experiment” where people of many faiths could live in peace. Later, the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were written in its largest city, the Battle of Gettysburg was fought on its farmland, and its coal, oil, and steel helped power the nation.
topics.answerHtml: Pennsylvania (accept Commonwealth of Pennsylvania or Province of Pennsylvania; do not accept “Philadelphia”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1737, the sons of this colony’s founder used a disputed old deed to claim Lenape [“leh-NAH-pay”] land as far as a man could walk in a day and a half, then hired fast runners to cover as much ground as possible. That deal is known as the Walking Purchase.
tossups.r: This colony’s Quaker founder called it a “Holy Experiment.” For 10 points, name this colony founded by William Penn.

tossups.p: Benjamin West painted this colony’s founder making a treaty of friendship with Lenape leaders beneath an elm tree at Shackamaxon [“shack-uh-MAX-un”]. King Charles II had given that founder this colony in 1681 to pay off a large debt that the king owed to the founder’s father, an admiral.
tossups.r: The colony’s name means “Penn’s Woods.” For 10 points, name this colony founded by the Quaker William Penn.

tossups.p: In 1688, Francis Daniel Pastorius and three neighbors in Germantown signed a Quaker petition that was one of the earliest protests against slavery in the English colonies. Almost a century later, in 1780, this state passed a law to gradually abolish slavery, one of the first such laws in the new nation.
tossups.r: Its largest city, Philadelphia, later became a key stop on the Underground Railroad. For 10 points, name this state founded by William Penn.

tossups.p: Every fifth mile along one boundary, surveyors set “crownstones” carved with the coat of arms of this colony’s proprietors on one side and that of Maryland’s Calvert family on the other. Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon surveyed that line from 1763 to 1767 to end a long border dispute.
tossups.r: That line later came to divide the free North from the slaveholding South. For 10 points, name this state north of the Mason–Dixon Line.

tossups.p: In 1754, a young George Washington surrendered Fort Necessity, in what is now this state, to French troops. Four years later, as British forces under John Forbes approached, the French destroyed their Fort Duquesne [“doo-KANE”] at the forks of the Ohio River, and the British built Fort Pitt there.
tossups.r: Fort Pitt grew into the city of Pittsburgh. For 10 points, name this state whose capital is Harrisburg.

tossups.p: After beating George Washington at Brandywine Creek in September 1777, William Howe’s army captured this state’s largest city. Washington’s surprise attack at Germantown failed weeks later, and his army then spent a hard winter at Valley Forge, where Baron von Steuben drilled the troops.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state where the Declaration of Independence was signed, in Philadelphia.

tossups.p: While British troops held the American capital in 1777, the Continental Congress met for one day in Lancaster and then moved to York, where it approved the Articles of Confederation. Lancaster later served as this state’s capital from 1799 to 1812.
tossups.r: Then the capital moved to Harrisburg. For 10 points, name this state, the second to ratify the U.S. Constitution.

tossups.p: John Adams pardoned John Fries [“FREEZ”], who had led farmers in this state’s southeast in a 1799 revolt against a federal tax on houses and land. Five years earlier, President George Washington had led militia troops into this state to end a revolt in its western counties against a tax on liquor.
tossups.r: That 1794 revolt was the Whiskey Rebellion. For 10 points, name this state, home to the cities of Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.

tossups.p: In 1864, Confederate cavalry burned much of Chambersburg in this state after the town failed to pay a ransom. A year earlier, Joshua Chamberlain’s 20th Maine had held Little Round Top in this state during a three-day battle that ended with the failure of Pickett’s Charge.
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln later gave a famous address at that battlefield. For 10 points, name this state, where Gettysburg is located.

tossups.p: Ida Tarbell grew up in this state’s oil region, where Standard Oil’s tactics hurt small businesses like her father’s, before writing a famous 1904 exposé of that company. That oil boom began in 1859, when Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial oil well in the United States near Titusville.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, whose other industries included coal mining and steelmaking around Pittsburgh.

tossups.p: In the late 1870s, about twenty Irish-American men accused of belonging to a secret society of coal miners called the Molly Maguires were executed in this state. In 1902, Theodore Roosevelt threatened to have the army run this state’s anthracite [“AN-thruh-site”] coal mines unless the owners agreed to settle a long strike.
tossups.r: Its capital is Harrisburg. For 10 points, name this coal-rich state, whose largest city is Philadelphia.

tossups.p: Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards during the 1892 Homestead Strike at one of Andrew Carnegie’s steel mills in this state. Those mills grew up near the point where the Allegheny [“al-uh-GAY-nee”] and Monongahela [“muh-non-guh-HEE-luh”] Rivers join to form the Ohio River.
tossups.r: That point is in the “Steel City,” Pittsburgh. For 10 points, name this state, whose capital is Harrisburg.

tossups.p: In 1889, the South Fork Dam above Johnstown in this state failed after heavy rains, and the flood that followed killed more than 2,000 people. Ninety years later, a partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant became the most serious accident in the history of U.S. commercial nuclear power.
tossups.r: That plant lies on the Susquehanna River near this state’s capital, Harrisburg. For 10 points, name this “Keystone State.”

tossups.p: In 1792, this state bought a small triangle of land from the federal government to gain a port on Lake Erie. During the War of 1812, Oliver Hazard Perry’s fleet was built at that port before Perry won the Battle of Lake Erie.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, whose eastern border with New Jersey is formed by the Delaware River.

tossups.p: Every February 2, crowds gather at Gobbler’s Knob in this state’s town of Punxsutawney [“punk-suh-TAW-nee”] to see whether a groundhog named Phil sees his shadow. Milton Hershey built a chocolate factory and a whole town for its workers in this state, where many Amish families farm in Lancaster County.
tossups.r: It is one of four states officially called a commonwealth. For 10 points, name this “Keystone State,” whose capital is Harrisburg.

clues.t: Founded by the Quaker William Penn (charter 1681) as a “Holy Experiment” in religious freedom
Nicknamed the “Keystone State”; officially one of four U.S. commonwealths
Capital: Harrisburg; largest city: Philadelphia; Pittsburgh lies in the west
Site of the Battle of Gettysburg (July 1–3, 1863) and Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address
Its name means “Penn’s Woods,” honoring William Penn’s father, an admiral to whom King Charles II owed money
The Mason–Dixon Line (1763–1767), marked with “crownstones,” settled its border with Maryland and later came to divide North from South
Revolution: Washington lost at Brandywine and Germantown (1777), then spent the winter at Valley Forge (1777–1778)
Whiskey Rebellion (1794): farmers in its western counties revolted against a federal tax on whiskey
Second state to ratify the Constitution (December 12, 1787), after Delaware
Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial oil well in the U.S. near Titusville (1859)
Pittsburgh became the “Steel City”; the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet there to form the Ohio
Three Mile Island (1979), near Harrisburg, was the worst accident in U.S. commercial nuclear power
Walking Purchase (1737): Penn’s sons claimed Lenape land as far as a man could walk in a day and a half
Benjamin West painted Penn’s treaty of friendship with the Lenape under an elm at Shackamaxon
Germantown Quakers signed an early protest against slavery (1688); a 1780 law began gradually abolishing slavery
Washington surrendered Fort Necessity (1754); Fort Duquesne at the forks of the Ohio became Fort Pitt (1758)
Congress met for a day in Lancaster, then in York, where it approved the Articles of Confederation (1777); Lancaster was the state capital 1799–1812
Confederate cavalry burned much of Chambersburg (1864) after the town failed to pay a ransom
Fries’s Rebellion (1799): John Adams pardoned John Fries, who led a revolt against a tax on houses and land
Ida Tarbell grew up in its oil region and exposed Standard Oil in 1904
Molly Maguires: about twenty Irish-American men accused of membership were executed in the late 1870s; Theodore Roosevelt stepped into the 1902 anthracite coal strike
Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards in the 1892 Homestead Strike at a Carnegie steel mill
Johnstown Flood (1889): the South Fork Dam failed, and more than 2,000 people died
Bought the Erie Triangle (1792) for a port on Lake Erie; Oliver Hazard Perry’s fleet was built there (1813)
Groundhog Day at Punxsutawney; Milton Hershey’s chocolate town; Amish farms in Lancaster County

trap.title: State or colony, not city
trap.body: Philadelphia was Penn’s capital and the home of the Continental Congress, so it is tempting to blurt out the city on a state question. In quiz bowl, Philadelphia is its own answer line: Liberty Bell, Independence Hall, and Constitutional Convention clues usually point to the city. Neighbors are another trap: Maryland (the Calverts and the Mason–Dixon Line), Delaware (once part of Penn’s lands), and New Jersey (across the Delaware River) all show up in Pennsylvania tossups.
trap.fix: Listen for “this state” or “this colony” versus “this city.” William Penn’s charter, Harrisburg, Gettysburg, Valley Forge, Pittsburgh, coal, oil, and steel all mean Pennsylvania; answer “Philadelphia” only when the question asks for a city.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pennsylvania (accept Commonwealth of Pennsylvania or Province of Pennsylvania; do not accept “Philadelphia”)

topics.name: Plessy v. Ferguson
topics.kicker: 1896 Supreme Court case · Upheld “separate but equal” segregation
topics.briefing: In 1892, Homer Plessy bought a first-class train ticket in New Orleans and sat in a car reserved for white passengers, on purpose, so that he could be arrested and challenge Louisiana’s law segregating trains. In 1896, the Supreme Court ruled 7–1 against him, approving “separate but equal” facilities. Justice John Marshall Harlan’s lone dissent declared that “our Constitution is color-blind,” and in 1954 _Brown v. Board of Education_ overturned the ruling for public schools.
topics.answerHtml: Plessy v. Ferguson (prompt on “Homer Plessy”; do not accept “Brown v. Board of Education”)
reject: brown v board of education of topeka

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A New Orleans group called the Comité des Citoyens [“koh-mee-TAY day see-twah-YEN”], or Citizens’ Committee, raised money to bring this case, and newspaper publisher Louis Martinet helped recruit the white Northern lawyer Albion Tourgée [“toor-ZHAY”] to argue it. The case challenged a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1896 Supreme Court case that upheld the doctrine of “separate but equal.”

tossups.p: This case began on June 7, 1892, when a passenger who had bought a first-class ticket on the East Louisiana Railroad sat in a car reserved for white riders and refused to move. He was arrested under the Separate Car Act of 1890, which required “equal but separate” train cars for white and Black passengers.
tossups.r: The Court ruled 7–1 against the passenger. For 10 points, name this 1896 Supreme Court case that upheld segregation on Louisiana trains.

tossups.p: A lone dissent in this case predicted that the ruling would prove just as harmful as the _Dred Scott_ decision and warned that the “thin disguise” of equal train cars would fool no one. That dissent was written by a Kentucky justice from a slaveholding family.
tossups.r: That justice, John Marshall Harlan, wrote that “our Constitution is color-blind.” For 10 points, name this 1896 case that upheld “separate but equal” segregation.

tossups.p: Writing for the majority in this case, Justice Henry Billings Brown argued that laws separating the races did not mark one race as inferior and that laws were powerless to change people’s social feelings. Brown said a state could use its “police power” to pass such reasonable rules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1896 case, later overturned in public schools by _Brown v. Board of Education_.

tossups.p: After this case’s plaintiff was arrested, his lawyers asked a New Orleans criminal court judge to throw out the charges because the train law was unconstitutional, but the judge refused. The Louisiana Supreme Court agreed with that judge, so the plaintiff appealed to the highest court in the nation.
tossups.r: That judge was John Howard Ferguson. For 10 points, name this 1896 case that upheld “separate but equal.”

tossups.p: In 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote for a unanimous Court that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,” rejecting this earlier decision’s reasoning for public schools. Thurgood Marshall of the NAACP had argued against this earlier decision’s doctrine in that 1954 case.
tossups.r: That case was _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this 1896 case that had allowed segregation under the rule of “separate but equal.”

tossups.p: This case’s plaintiff, a shoemaker with mostly European ancestry, was classified as Black under Louisiana law, which helped his lawyers argue that sorting people by race made no sense. Many railroads disliked the law he challenged because the extra cars cost money, and his arrest was arranged in advance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1896 Supreme Court case that began with a planned arrest on a New Orleans train.

tossups.p: Lawyers in this case argued that a segregation law brought back a mark of slavery banned by the Thirteenth Amendment and denied equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. The majority rejected both arguments, saying the Fourteenth Amendment protected political equality but could not force social mixing of the races.
tossups.r: The Court’s vote was 7–1. For 10 points, name this 1896 decision that upheld Louisiana’s “separate but equal” railroad law.

tossups.p: One of this case’s lawyers, a former Union soldier, had written _A Fool’s Errand_, a best-selling novel about Reconstruction in North Carolina. That lawyer also argued that a reputation for being white was a form of property that a train conductor could not take away.
tossups.r: In his brief, that lawyer, Albion Tourgée [“toor-ZHAY”], wrote that the law should be “color-blind.” For 10 points, name this 1896 case that upheld segregated train cars in Louisiana.

tossups.p: Members of the families of this case’s plaintiff and its trial judge formed a foundation together to teach about it, and in 2022 Louisiana’s governor granted the plaintiff a posthumous pardon. After losing his appeal, the plaintiff had pleaded guilty and paid a 25-dollar fine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1896 Supreme Court case that established the doctrine of “separate but equal.”

tossups.p: In the 1950 case _Sweatt v. Painter_, the Court ruled that a law school Texas had quickly set up for Black students was not equal to the University of Texas, chipping away at this earlier decision. Thurgood Marshall argued that 1950 case before winning an even bigger victory four years later.
tossups.r: That 1954 victory overturned this 1896 decision for public schools. For 10 points, name this case that allowed “separate but equal” segregation.

tossups.p: The only justice to dissent in this case had also cast the only dissent in the Civil Rights Cases of 1883, earning the nickname “the Great Dissenter.” His grandson, who had the same name, served on the same court from 1955 to 1971.
tossups.r: That justice, John Marshall Harlan, wrote that “our Constitution is color-blind.” For 10 points, name this 1896 case that upheld segregated train cars.

tossups.p: The majority opinion in this case pointed to an 1850 Massachusetts ruling that had allowed separate schools for Black children in Boston as proof that such laws were reasonable. Justice David Brewer did not take part in this case, which was decided 7–1.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1896 decision that upheld Louisiana’s segregated train cars under the rule of “separate but equal.”

tossups.p: A historical marker stands near the Press Street railroad crossing in New Orleans, where this case’s plaintiff was arrested after telling the conductor he would not move to the car for Black passengers. He had bought a first-class ticket to Covington, Louisiana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1896 Supreme Court case that upheld Louisiana’s law requiring segregated train cars.

tossups.p: For 58 years, this decision gave legal backing to Jim Crow laws that kept Black and white Americans apart in schools, restaurants, theaters, and even at drinking fountains across the South. Facilities set aside for Black Americans under those laws were almost always worse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1896 case that said segregated facilities were legal if they were “separate but equal.”

clues.t: 1896 Supreme Court case that upheld racial segregation under the doctrine of “separate but equal”
Began when a Black passenger in Louisiana sat in a train car reserved for white riders and was arrested (1892)
Overturned for public schools by _Brown v. Board of Education_ (1954)
John Marshall Harlan’s lone dissent: “Our Constitution is color-blind”
Challenged Louisiana’s Separate Car Act (1890), which required “equal but separate” train cars
Decided 7–1 on May 18, 1896
Justice Henry Billings Brown wrote the majority opinion, arguing that separating the races did not mark one race as inferior
Gave legal backing to Jim Crow segregation laws across the South for 58 years
Trial judge John Howard Ferguson of New Orleans refused to throw out the charges
The Court said the law did not violate the 14th Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause or the 13th Amendment
New Orleans’s Comité des Citoyens (Citizens’ Committee) planned the test case; Louis Martinet helped organize it
Lawyer Albion Tourgée, author of _A Fool’s Errand_, argued that the law should be “color-blind”
Arrested June 7, 1892, on the East Louisiana Railroad near Press Street in New Orleans, with a first-class ticket to Covington
The plaintiff, a shoemaker with mostly European ancestry, was classified as Black; railroads disliked the law’s extra cost
Harlan warned the ruling would prove as harmful as the _Dred Scott_ decision; the “thin disguise” of equal cars would fool no one
Harlan, from a Kentucky slaveholding family, also dissented alone in the Civil Rights Cases (1883): “the Great Dissenter”
Majority: states could use their “police power” to pass reasonable laws, and the law could not force social equality
The majority cited an 1850 Massachusetts ruling allowing separate schools in Boston; Justice David Brewer did not take part
In _Brown_ (1954), Earl Warren wrote that “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal”; Thurgood Marshall argued that case
_Sweatt v. Painter_ (1950): a hastily built Texas law school for Black students was ruled not equal
The plaintiff paid a $25 fine (1897); relatives on both sides formed a foundation, and Louisiana pardoned him in 2022

trap.title: Upheld or struck down?
trap.body: Tossups on _Brown v. Board of Education_ almost always mention Plessy v. Ferguson as the case it overturned, and Plessy tossups mention Brown, so it is easy to name the wrong one. It gets trickier: the justice who wrote the Plessy majority opinion was named Henry Billings Brown, and Plessy was about train cars, not schools. Answering “separate but equal” names the doctrine, not the case, and does not earn credit.
trap.fix: 1896, Louisiana trains, New Orleans, Albion Tourgée, John Marshall Harlan’s lone dissent, and segregation upheld mean Plessy v. Ferguson. 1954, schools in Topeka, Earl Warren, Thurgood Marshall, a unanimous Court, and segregation struck down mean _Brown v. Board of Education_.
trap.line: Real answer line: Plessy v. Ferguson (prompt on “Homer Plessy”; do not accept “Brown v. Board of Education”)

topics.name: Robert E. Lee
topics.kicker: Confederate general · Led the Army of Northern Virginia
topics.briefing: Robert E. Lee graduated second in his West Point class without a single demerit and became one of the U.S. Army’s most respected officers. When Virginia left the Union in 1861, he turned down an offer to command a Union army and instead led the Confederacy’s Army of Northern Virginia, winning battles like Chancellorsville before losing at Gettysburg. On April 9, 1865, he surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, and he spent his last years as a college president.
topics.answerHtml: Robert E. Lee (or Robert Edward Lee; do not accept “Henry Lee” or “Richard Henry Lee”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man’s father, a Revolutionary War cavalry hero nicknamed “Light-Horse Harry,” praised George Washington in a eulogy as “first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen.” This man was born at Stratford Hall in Virginia and graduated second in the West Point class of 1829 without a single demerit.
tossups.r: He later surrendered at Appomattox Court House. For 10 points, name this Virginian who commanded the Confederacy’s Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: As a young Army engineer, this man helped redirect the Mississippi River’s current to save the harbor at St. Louis. During the Mexican-American War, he found a hidden path around the Mexican army at Cerro Gordo [“SAIR-oh GOR-doh”], helping Winfield Scott win that battle.
tossups.r: He later led the Army of Northern Virginia. For 10 points, name this Confederate general who surrendered at Appomattox.

tossups.p: In 1882, the Supreme Court ruled that the U.S. government had illegally taken this man’s family estate, and the government then bought it from his son for 150,000 dollars. During the Civil War, Quartermaster General Montgomery Meigs had begun burying Union soldiers on that estate, which belonged to this man’s wife, a great-granddaughter of Martha Washington.
tossups.r: That estate became Arlington National Cemetery. For 10 points, name this Confederate general who commanded the Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: A few years after serving as superintendent of West Point, this officer commanded the force of U.S. Marines that captured John Brown at Harpers Ferry in 1859. Lieutenant J. E. B. Stuart, who later led his cavalry, served as his aide there.
tossups.r: Two years later, he joined the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this general who led the Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: In April 1861, Francis Preston Blair offered this man command of a major Union army on behalf of Abraham Lincoln. This man turned the offer down and resigned from the U.S. Army after his home state left the Union, explaining that he could not fight against Virginia.
tossups.r: He instead joined the Confederacy and led the Army of Northern Virginia. For 10 points, name this general.

tossups.p: Early in the Civil War, this general was mocked as “Granny” after a failed campaign in western Virginia and as the “King of Spades” for having his men dig trenches around Richmond. He took command of the main Confederate army in Virginia in June 1862, after Joseph E. Johnston was wounded at Seven Pines.
tossups.r: He then drove George McClellan away from Richmond in the Seven Days Battles. For 10 points, name this commander of the Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: Near Frederick, Maryland, Union soldiers found a copy of this general’s Special Order 191 wrapped around three cigars, revealing his plans. Days later, in September 1862, his army fought George McClellan along Antietam [“an-TEE-tum”] Creek, in the bloodiest single day in American history.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Confederate general whose first invasion of the North ended at Antietam.

tossups.p: While watching the fighting at Fredericksburg in December 1862, this general reportedly said, “It is well that war is so terrible, or we should grow too fond of it.” His army turned back Ambrose Burnside’s repeated attacks on Marye’s Heights in that battle.
tossups.r: He later surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant. For 10 points, name this commander of the Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: Though outnumbered more than two to one, this general split his army and sent Stonewall Jackson around Joseph Hooker’s right flank in May 1863. After Jackson was accidentally shot by his own men, this general sent word that Jackson had lost his left arm, “but I have lost my right.”
tossups.r: That battle was Chancellorsville. For 10 points, name this Confederate general, who lost at Gettysburg two months later.

tossups.p: This general lacked good scouting reports because J. E. B. Stuart’s cavalry was off riding around the Union army, and he overruled James Longstreet’s objections before ordering a massive attack on the Union center. After that attack failed, he told his returning soldiers, “It’s all my fault.”
tossups.r: That July 1863 attack was Pickett’s Charge, at Gettysburg. For 10 points, name this Confederate commander who had invaded Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: In February 1865, this man was finally named general in chief of all Confederate armies, while his own army was trapped in a long siege at Petersburg. In 1864, he had fought the Union’s Overland Campaign at the Wilderness, Spotsylvania, and Cold Harbor.
tossups.r: In April 1865, he surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant. For 10 points, name this commander of the Army of Northern Virginia.

tossups.p: This general surrendered in the parlor of Wilmer McLean, whose earlier home had stood on the battlefield of the First Battle of Bull Run. In his farewell message, General Order No. 9, this general told his soldiers they had been “compelled to yield to overwhelming numbers and resources.”
tossups.r: That surrender took place at Appomattox Court House in April 1865. For 10 points, name this general who surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant.

tossups.p: After the Civil War, this man became president of Washington College in Lexington, Virginia, which was renamed after his death to honor both him and George Washington. His beloved gray horse, Traveller, is buried near the chapel on that campus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former Confederate general who surrendered at Appomattox Court House.

tossups.p: In 1970, an archivist found this man’s long-lost loyalty oath, which he had signed in 1865 as part of a request for a pardon. In 1975, President Gerald Ford signed a resolution passed by Congress restoring this man’s full rights of citizenship.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Confederate general who had surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox.

tossups.p: In August 1862, this general’s army beat John Pope’s Union army at the Second Battle of Bull Run, after Stonewall Jackson’s men seized the Union supply base at Manassas Junction. A few weeks later, this general led his first invasion of the North, into Maryland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who commanded the Army of Northern Virginia from 1862 to 1865.

clues.t: Commanded the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia (1862–1865) during the Civil War
Surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865
Lost the Battle of Gettysburg (July 1863), his second invasion of the North, when Pickett’s Charge failed
Chancellorsville (May 1863): split his army to beat Joseph Hooker; Stonewall Jackson was accidentally shot by his own men and died
His first invasion of the North ended at Antietam (September 1862), the bloodiest single day in American history
Led the U.S. Marines who captured John Brown at Harpers Ferry (1859)
His wife’s estate across the Potomac from Washington became Arlington National Cemetery
Turned down command of a Union army (April 1861) and resigned from the U.S. Army when Virginia seceded
Took command in June 1862 after Joseph E. Johnston was wounded at Seven Pines; drove McClellan from Richmond in the Seven Days Battles
After the war, president of Washington College in Lexington, Virginia, which was renamed to honor him too
His famous gray horse was named Traveller
Born at Stratford Hall, Virginia (1807); his father, “Light-Horse Harry,” eulogized Washington as “first in war, first in peace…”
Graduated second in the West Point class of 1829 with no demerits; later West Point’s superintendent (1852–1855)
As an Army engineer, saved St. Louis’s harbor on the Mississippi; scouted a path around Mexican lines at Cerro Gordo (1847)
Wife Mary Custis was a great-granddaughter of Martha Washington; Montgomery Meigs began burials at her estate, and an 1882 court ruling said it was illegally taken
Francis Preston Blair offered him command of a Union army on Lincoln’s behalf (April 1861)
Mocked early in the war as “Granny” and as the “King of Spades” (for digging trenches around Richmond)
Union soldiers found his Special Order 191 (the “Lost Order”) wrapped around three cigars near Frederick, Maryland
At Fredericksburg (1862): “It is well that war is so terrible, or we should grow too fond of it”
Of the wounded Stonewall Jackson: “He has lost his left arm, but I have lost my right”
After Pickett’s Charge failed: “It’s all my fault”; J. E. B. Stuart’s cavalry had been away, and Longstreet had objected
Named general in chief of all Confederate armies (February 1865) during the Siege of Petersburg
Surrendered in Wilmer McLean’s parlor; his farewell, General Order No. 9, cited “overwhelming numbers and resources”
His lost 1865 loyalty oath was found in 1970; Gerald Ford restored his full citizenship rights in 1975
Beat John Pope at the Second Battle of Bull Run (August 1862)

trap.title: Which Lee, which general?
trap.body: Several famous Lees show up in quiz bowl: Robert E. Lee; his father, Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee, a Revolutionary War cavalry leader; Richard Henry Lee, who proposed independence in 1776; and the novelist Harper Lee. Civil War tossups add another trap, because Stonewall Jackson, James Longstreet, and J. E. B. Stuart served under Robert E. Lee and are named in the same questions.
trap.fix: Revolution and Declaration clues mean one of the other Lees, and _To Kill a Mockingbird_ means Harper Lee. In a Civil War tossup, “this commander” of the whole Army of Northern Virginia is Robert E. Lee; the general shot by his own men at Chancellorsville is Stonewall Jackson, and the Union general who accepted the surrender at Appomattox is Ulysses S. Grant.
trap.line: Real answer line: Robert E(dward) Lee (do not accept “Henry Lee” or “Richard Henry Lee”)
